patient.chief_complaint: Brought in unresponsive after witnessed fall, rhythmic arm movements, history of Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease concern — family alarmed by EEG report mentioning 'typical CJD pattern'
patient.history_present_illness: A 67-year-old White female retired teacher was brought to the emergency department by her adult son after a witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure followed by failure to return to normal consciousness over 90 minutes. She has a 3-month history of rapidly progressive dementia — she went from mild cognitive complaints to being unable to recognize her son and needing full-time care. Her neurologist has been evaluating her for suspected prion disease (Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease). A brain MRI done 4 weeks ago reportedly showed 'cortical ribboning.' Her neurologist had recently mentioned sporadic CJD was probable per the Paris-Edinburgh criteria. She was not started on any specific treatment (none available for CJD). She takes quetiapine for behavioral symptoms and escitalopram for concurrent depression diagnosed before the dementia. On admission she is unresponsive, making occasional groaning sounds. Her son is very distressed because the previous hospital's EEG was reported as showing 'generalized periodic sharp wave complexes at 1 Hz — typical CJD pattern, highly supportive of prion disease.' The son asks whether the 'seizures' require treatment or whether this is 'just the CJD.'

past_medical_history: Suspected sporadic Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (sCJD) — diagnosis probable per Paris-Edinburgh criteria
family_history: Mother: Alzheimer's dementia. Father: died of stroke. No known family history of CJD or prion disease. Son healthy.

social_history.note: Retired teacher. Widowed, lives with son. Non-smoker, no alcohol, no illicit drugs. Previously highly functional.

neurological_exam.mental_status: GCS 6 (E2V1M3). Unresponsive post-seizure at 90 minutes. Eyes open briefly to pain only. No verbal response. Extensor posturing to noxious stimuli.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils 3 mm bilaterally, sluggishly reactive. Blink reflex present. Oculocephalic reflex present. No gag reflex.
neurological_exam.motor: Intermittent myoclonic jerks of both arms irregularly. No purposeful movement. Extensor posturing bilaterally to noxious stimuli. Diffuse increased tone.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Diffusely brisk reflexes bilaterally. Bilateral Babinski present.
neurological_exam.additional: Known probable sCJD (Paris-Edinburgh criteria). Post-ictal 90 minutes. Groaning sounds only. Myoclonic jerks may represent CJD myoclonus vs superimposed NCSE — EEG required to distinguish.

results.title: Sporadic Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease: clinical features, diagnostic criteria, and EEG characteristics
results.key_finding: Sporadic CJD is characterized by rapid neurological decline. EEG findings include generalised periodic sharp wave complexes (PSWCs) at approximately 1 Hz, reported as a supportive diagnostic criterion in established criteria. DWI cortical ribboning and thalamic/basal ganglia signal change are the characteristic imaging findings. RT-QuIC assay sensitivity and specificity for prion disease have been reported in multiple validation studies. The co-occurrence of focal ictal EEG patterns on a PSWC background has been described in case series.

output.summary: Published literature on sporadic CJD documents clinical diagnostic criteria (including EEG, MRI, and CSF biomarker criteria), RT-QuIC performance characteristics, and the electrographic features of CJD-associated PSWCs versus superimposed ictal patterns. The existence of two coexisting EEG patterns in CJD patients has been described. Antiseizure medication use for intercurrent ictal activity in this population is reported in case series and retrospective cohorts.

results.title: Palliative care in prion disease: clinical features and symptom burden
results.key_finding: Prion disease is uniformly fatal. Published literature describes the symptom burden — including myoclonus, agitation, dyspnea, and altered consciousness — encountered across the disease course. The prevalence of intercurrent complications (including infection and ictal events) in this population and their impact on patient comfort have been reviewed in observational cohorts.

output.summary: Published evidence on palliative care in prion disease describes the natural history of sCJD, symptom prevalence across the disease course, and published experience with symptom management approaches reported in the literature. Goals-of-care frameworks and hospice utilization patterns in this population are described in observational studies.

useless_tools.rationale: No clinical suspicion of cardiac source of embolus or cardiogenic seizure; routine echo is not indicated in SE workup absent cardiac findings.
No suspicion of arrhythmogenic syncope or cardiac comorbidity precipitating SE; routine telemetry beyond standard ICU monitoring adds cost without yield.
Amyloid PET has no role in acute SE evaluation; dementia biomarker imaging does not change acute management.
Carotid duplex is for ischemic stroke workup; SE without focal vascular suspicion does not warrant carotid imaging.
DaTscan / dopamine transporter imaging has no role in SE; no parkinsonism question relevant to acute management.
Neuropsych battery cannot be performed in encephalopathic prion patient.

contraindicated_actions: Do NOT escalate to deep anesthetic infusion in confirmed terminal sCJD without goals-of-care alignment
Do NOT skip autoimmune encephalitis workup — treatable mimics share clinical features with prion disease
Do NOT treat the EEG PSWCs as NCSE — these are the CJD signature, not seizures
Avoid anesthetic infusion (midazolam/propofol/pentobarbital) for refractory SE in confirmed terminal sCJD — goals of care favor comfort; aggressive escalation not aligned with prognosis.
key_reasoning_points: Periodic sharp wave complexes are pathognomonic of sCJD and are NOT seizures — distinguish from concurrent focal NCSE
RT-QuIC has very high sensitivity and specificity for prion disease
Autoimmune encephalitis (LGI1, CASPR2) can mimic rapidly progressive dementia — must be excluded as a treatable mimic
Goals-of-care must inform SE escalation in terminal prion disease
